name: PT Steady Safe Tbk

frontmatter.title: Steady Safe: a repaired balance sheet, a compressed margin and a float that sets the price
frontmatter.summary: SAFE runs buses for TransJakarta. Debt is gone, cash is building, but the first nine months of 2026 show revenue growing while margins compress. FY2025 revenue fell -10.3% on fewer kilometres. Our fundamental value sits well below the price; the konglo lens, not the business, produces the HOLD.
thesis: The balance sheet is repaired: debt fell from IDR185.4bn in FY2022 to IDR2.1bn in FY2025, equity is positive at IDR63.6bn and the company holds net cash of IDR-21.3bn [S4].
The earnings trend has turned: nine-month 2026 revenue rose to IDR169.6bn from IDR160.3bn, but direct costs and operating expenses grew faster and operating profit fell to IDR24.7bn [S3].
Capacity is unused: 119 buses operate against a 319-unit quota, so volume is the only growth lever and the single customer controls it [S2].
At Rp660 the shares trade at 1.52 times our fundamental value of Rp435; the target of Rp646 rests on the float lens, not on the business [S8].

catalysts.event: FY2026 audited results: whether the margin compression of the first nine months continues into the fourth quarter
End of the MSCI consultation feedback period on Standalone status for Indonesia
MSCI decision on moving Indonesia to Standalone status
Free-float deadline: SAFE must move from its current float to the new minimum; the controller must sell or dilute

blocks.text: **HOLD, target Rp646 against a price of Rp660, a return of -2.1%.** Our fundamental value is Rp435 a share today and Rp486 in twelve months; the target sits between the two because the konglo lens assumes a controlled, thinly traded stock closes only part of the gap between price and value within a year. The gap here is a premium, not a discount, and we are not paying it with a business case: on fundamentals alone the shares are worth less than they cost, so this HOLD is produced by the float lens, not by the business.

PT Steady Safe Tbk is a Jakarta bus operator. It runs 119 Volvo buses on the TransJakarta busway network under a cooperation agreement with PT Transportasi Jakarta, the city-owned operator, and it is paid essentially per kilometre travelled [S2]. FY2025 revenue was IDR209.6bn on 9.2 million kilometres, a fall of -10.3% [S2]. The company is small: 50.0 employees, a market capitalisation of IDR542.0bn and three-month average daily turnover of IDR840.0m [S0].

What changed first was the balance sheet. Debt fell from IDR185.4bn at the end of FY2022 to IDR2.1bn at the end of FY2025 as the bus financing with PT Indomobil Finance was repaid [S2][S4]. Equity, negative at IDR-57.3bn in FY2022, is now IDR63.6bn, helped by IDR20.6bn of new paid-in capital and a common-control restructuring difference credited directly to equity [S4]. Interest expense fell from IDR32.0bn to IDR1.6bn, which is why net profit rose to IDR39.5bn even as revenue fell [S0][S4].

What changed second is the margin, and this is where we differ from a simple balance-sheet story. In the first nine months of 2026 revenue rose to IDR169.6bn from IDR160.3bn a year earlier, yet direct expenses rose faster at IDR123.4bn and operating expenses by nearly a third, leaving operating profit at IDR24.7bn [S3]. The depreciation charge inside direct costs is fixed, so the pressure sits in the cash cost of running buses at a tariff that has not been reset [S3].

The variant view is therefore not that the company is cheap. It is that the market has re-rated a repaired but single-customer contractor to 20.9 times our FY2026 earnings and 7.1 times EV/EBITDA on our FY2026 estimates (year-end net cash), or 7.0 times on the current net cash and trailing EBITDA, on a 6.4% float that leaves the marginal price to be set by a handful of holders [S0]. Three things move the value: the kilometre allocation, which the customer sets; the tariff, which the customer also sets; and the float, where the 28.5-month deadline to reach the new minimum creates supply that a stock with our turnover cannot absorb quietly [S8].

SAFE operates buses, not a network. Under the cooperation agreement with PT Transportasi Jakarta, the company supplies vehicles, drivers and maintenance, and is compensated on kilometres actually travelled at an agreed rate; maintenance cost is itself calculated as an agreed tariff multiplied by realised kilometres [S2]. That makes the P&L an almost pure function of two variables the company does not control: the kilometre allocation and the tariff.

The operating history is one of managed decline in volume. Kilometres travelled were 9.2 million km in FY2025 against 9.9 million km in FY2024, which the annual report attributes to TransJakarta's operating-performance policies, buses stopped for technical faults, accident-related unit reductions and driver turnover [S2]. Revenue fell faster than kilometres because the blended realisation per kilometre also slipped [S2].

Capacity is the asset. A Jakarta Transportation Agency decree issued in 2022 gives the company a quota of 319 buses to operate on the TransJakarta network, of which it has realised 119 Volvo units, with the balance to be procured in stages as operating readiness allows [S2]. Revenue per bus is therefore not a market price but an administrative allocation, and the difference between the operating fleet and the quota is the company's only large growth option.

Cost structure is heavy and largely fixed. Direct costs were IDR148.5bn in FY2025 and they include bus depreciation, which the notes place inside direct expenses while other depreciation sits in operating expenses [S4]. We restate depreciation at IDR30.6bn for FY2025 from the accumulated-depreciation roll-forward, which is why our EBITDA of IDR74.0bn is far above the data pack's near-zero figure [S4]. Operating expenses were IDR17.8bn in FY2025, roughly a twelfth of revenue, and they rose sharply in 2026 [S4][S3].

The group is a controlled vehicle. PT Infiniti Wahana holds 56.5% of the shares, BNP Paribas Singapore Branch Wealth Management appears with 27.8% and PT Abdi Raharja with 7.5%, so three holders account for almost all the register [S2]. The company has one subsidiary and small associates, with minority stakes in two other TransJakarta operators that appear in the filings as co-shareholders rather than competitors [S4]. Management is thin - a president director, one director and a corporate secretary - and the filings disclose a single bus-operating segment, so the "Financial Services" label in the data pack is a legacy tag rather than a second business [S4].

Steady Safe is one of the older listed transport names in Jakarta, with a history that includes a debt-to-equity swap with Peregrine Fixed Income in 2002 and repeated non-preemptive share issuances. Its market following is retail and thin, which is consistent with the low institutional ownership shown in the market data.

The relevant market is not Indonesian logistics; it is the TransJakarta busway operating contract. TransJakarta is a city-owned public service obligation funded by the Jakarta provincial budget, and it procures capacity from private operators who own and run buses. Steady Safe is one of several such operators, alongside names such as Mayasari Bakti and Biro Perjalanan Wisata Pahala Kencana, which appear in the filings as co-shareholders in PT Jakarta Mega Trans [S4].

Demand for the service is political and budgetary rather than cyclical. The company's own disclosure of FY2025's shortfall names TransJakarta policy as the cause, including buses being sent home and fined when they break down mid-shift, which reduces achieved kilometres [S2]. That is the competitive dynamic in one sentence: the counterparty both allocates volume and penalises operational failure, and the operator carries the fleet risk.

Barriers to entry are moderate and mostly capital-based: a quota from the transportation agency, a bus fleet that meets the service standard (Pergub DKI No. 13 of 2019 sets the minimum service standards quoted in the report) [S2], and a driver pool. None of that creates pricing power. Switching costs exist for the city only in the sense that replacing a fleet operator takes time; for the operator, the single customer is the whole business.

Five forces, briefly. Supplier power is moderate: buses come from a small set of OEMs and financing has come from a single multifinance partner that has now been repaid [S2]. Buyer power is absolute, because one buyer sets both kilometres and tariffs. New entrants are constrained by the quota but not excluded, and the city can reallocate kilometres between operators. Substitutes are other Jakarta transit modes, which affect the city's budget rather than SAFE's tariff directly. Rivalry among operators is for allocation, not for customers.

The industry deck drivers we would normally use for this desk - freight rates, trade volumes, port throughput - do not apply to this name, and we say so rather than force a fit [S2]. SAFE is a regulated-service contractor whose revenue is a line in a provincial budget, so the useful external series are the Jakarta subsidy, the rupiah cost of spare parts and the policy rate that prices fleet finance. Our LOGISTICS_TRANSPORT peers (GMFI, BIRD, CASS, SMDR, TMAS) are loose comparables only: they carry freight or passenger demand risk, while SAFE carries budget and allocation risk [S0].

Moat assessment: none that we can evidence. The company holds a quota, not a franchise; the quota is a licence to operate at the city's discretion and the FY2025 kilometre cut shows that discretion being used [S2]. A moat would require either a cost advantage the filings do not show or a contract term that protects volume and tariff, and neither is disclosed. The compounder/quality method card is still the right frame, because the question is the durability of a small earnings stream, but its fade requirement bites here: with no moat mechanism to name, returns fade toward the cost of capital rather than being defended.

External influences that matter are the Jakarta budget and subsidy for TransJakarta, the rupiah (spare parts and any imported fleet are dollar-linked while revenue is rupiah), the policy rate that prices fleet financing, and the exchange's own rules on free float and index membership [S11]. The rupiah at 17,633 against the house FY2027E of 18,350 raises the rupiah cost of maintenance if the current-account pressure in the macro deck persists [S11].

History first, with the restatement that matters. The data pack shows depreciation near zero for FY2024 and FY2025, which cannot be right for a business whose net fixed assets were IDR144.4bn at the end of FY2025 and are IDR121.4bn at the third quarter of 2026 [S4][S3]. We take the charge from the fixed-asset roll-forward, IDR29.2bn in FY2024 and IDR30.6bn in FY2025, which lifts FY2025 EBITDA to IDR74.0bn and the margin to 35.3% [S4][S7]. Nothing about cash flow changes, but every EV/EBITDA comparison does.

Revenue fell from IDR242.8bn in FY2023 to IDR233.6bn in FY2024 and IDR209.6bn in FY2025, tracking kilometres down [S2]. Gross margin fell from 33.9% to 29.2% as volume fell against a cost base that includes depreciation and driver costs, and the operating margin fell from 27.8% to 20.7% [S2]. Below the line the story is entirely interest: the charge fell from IDR32.0bn to IDR1.6bn as the Indomobil facility was repaid, so pre-tax profit rose to IDR41.5bn and net profit to IDR39.5bn on a falling revenue base [S0][S4].

Cash generation is the strongest part of the case, and it has continued. Operating cash flow was IDR59.4bn in FY2025 and IDR42.1bn in the first nine months of 2026, helped by depreciation of IDR30.6bn that is a non-cash charge and by negative net working capital of IDR-84.9bn, where payables and accrued costs exceed receivables [S4][S3]. Capex was zero in FY2025 and zero again in the first nine months of 2026, so free cash flow equalled operating cash flow and the cash balance is on course for IDR86.6bn on our full-year estimate [S4][S3].

The first earnings-quality flag is the related-party flow. In a year in which SAFE raised IDR20.6bn of new paid-in capital and recognised a common-control restructuring difference of the same order, it also advanced IDR46.7bn to related parties, more than a fifth of revenue [S4]. We cannot see from the annual report what those advances financed, and the year-end balance was small because most of the flow reversed within the year: related-party other receivables were IDR1.5bn net at 30 September 2026 against an allowance of IDR5.0bn, so the company has already provided against most of the gross balance [S3]. The flow did not stop in 2026 - the nine-month investing cash flow shows a further IDR1.1bn advanced, in the same direction - but the stock is now small enough that we do not treat a write-off as a value event [S3].

Our forecast for FY2026 is built from the actual nine months rather than from the FY2025 trend. We assume revenue of IDR221.7bn, growth of 5.8% on FY2025, which annualises the run-rate already delivered rather than extrapolating it upward: the implied fourth quarter is the same year-on-year rate as the first nine months, not an acceleration, because Q4 2025 was seasonally weak and no tariff reset has been announced [S3]. Gross margin is 27.3%, the nine-month realisation, against 29.2% in FY2025; operating expenses are held at 12.7% of revenue, the nine-month figure [S3][S4]. The result is operating profit of IDR32.4bn and net profit of IDR26.0bn, with earnings per share of 31.6 against 48.1.

From FY2027 we assume revenue growth of 3.0%, then 2.0%, 1.0% and 1.0%: allocation-only growth with no volume from the unfilled quota, because the company has disclosed no funding plan for the unfilled quota and our capex line funds replacement of the existing fleet, not expansion [S2]. We let gross margin edge up to 27.5% as volume stabilises against a fixed depreciation charge while operating expenses ease to 12.2% once the 2026 step-up is lapped [S3][S4]. Depreciation stays at 14.5% of revenue, consistent with a fleet that is not changing, so EBITDA rises from IDR64.6bn to IDR70.9bn and the margin from 29.1% to 29.8% [S4].

Capex is the assumption the red team corrected, and it was wrong. The company spent nothing in FY2025 or in the first nine months of 2026 while net fixed assets fell from IDR144.4bn to IDR121.4bn, so we now hold FY2026 capex at nil, exactly the last actual, rather than the spend the first draft carried [S4][S3]. The ramp starts in FY2027 at 8.0% and reaches 14.5%, roughly the depreciation charge, from FY2028, which keeps the operating fleet whole without funding the quota expansion; that expansion has no disclosed funding plan, and if it happens the money will come from the controller or from new shares [S2]. Holding the FY2026 spend at nil instead of the earlier allowance adds that cash to the FY2026 free cash flow and is one of the reasons our DCF value is what it is; the later ramp to full replacement is the larger, negative, offset. Working capital stays negative but less so than in the nine-month 2026 balance sheet: we hold FY2026 at the FY2025 ratio of -40.5% of revenue, then let it ease gradually to -42.5% and -44.0% as the cash build against stretched payables slows [S4][S3]. This step removes a release (or creates a small draw) in FY2026, consistent with the observed path; the earlier three-year average created an unsourced working-capital release that would have represented about a third of FY2026 free cash flow - an optimism bias we now correct.

Balance sheet: net cash of IDR-21.3bn, equity of IDR63.6bn, book value per share of 77.4, and no debt maturities to refinance [S0]. Capital allocation is the weak link. With no dividend, no buyback and no disclosed expansion budget, cash accumulates and then moves to related parties, as it did in FY2025; the payout assumption is therefore zero for the forecast period, consistent with a company whose last distributions were stock dividends in the previous century [S2][S4].

Method set. A discounted cash flow is the primary method because the asset base is finite, the cash flows are contract-driven and the balance sheet is now clean enough for enterprise value to mean something. We weight DCF at 75%, EV/EBITDA at 10% and P/E at 15% [S0]. The DCF weight is higher than the first draft because both multiples capitalise trailing FY2025 earnings in a year the margin has already fallen, so they are cross-checks, not anchors. The compounder card's fade discipline applies: with no evidenced moat we fade returns toward the cost of capital, and we cap terminal growth at 2.0%, below the macro deck's 5.3% real GDP growth for Indonesia, because this is a Jakarta bus contract and not the Indonesian economy [S11].
Cost of capital.

We use a cost of equity of 11.9%, inside the house IDR band. The build, exactly as the engine computes it, is the rupiah risk-free proxy of 7.4% less the sovereign default spread of 1.6% (the spread is the part of the risk-free rate that is already country risk, so charging it twice would double-count), plus a levered beta of 0.9 times the sum of the mature-market premium of 4.2% and the country risk premium of 2.5% [S11]. With debt at IDR2.1bn the debt weight is nil and WACC equals the cost of equity at 11.9%. We do not add a separate size or float premium to the discount rate: the float is priced through the liquidity discount below, and charging both would be a hidden haircut.
Primary method.

The DCF values the existing operating fleet, an allocation-only revenue path to FY2030 and then a 2.0% terminal, and gives Rp461 a share before the liquidity adjustment, with the terminal value at 36.2% of the total [S0]. Two cross-checks disagree, and we say why.

EV/EBITDA gives Rp711, 54.3% versus the DCF, because it capitalises restated EBITDA of IDR74.0bn - the peak margin year - on a peer multiple of 7.2 times; the engine's LTM fallback takes the last restated fiscal year whenever the filing's scope differs from the data pack, and the peer multiples are themselves trailing, so the pairing is internally consistent but it is a peak-year number. On our own FY2026E EBITDA of IDR64.6bn the same multiple gives a materially lower value, which is why we cut the weight from a quarter to a tenth rather than letting a peak year carry the blend [S0][S4]. P/E gives Rp388, -15.7% versus the DCF, because it applies a low multiple to FY2025 earnings that were flattered by a collapsed interest line and by an unusually high gross margin. Each is a single-year snapshot of earnings that depend on an administrative allocation, and the DCF is the only method that charges the capex the business actually needs.
Sensitivity.

The value is carried by three inputs: the revenue growth path after FY2026, the gross margin and the discount rate. A one-point change in the gross margin moves value by more than a one-point change in terminal growth, because the cost base is fixed and the margin is where the 2026 compression sits. The bear case is not a demand collapse - Jakarta will still run buses - it is a tariff that is not reset while costs inflate, which is what the nine-month 2026 accounts already show beginning to happen [S3].

What the price implies. At Rp660 the reverse DCF says the market is pricing FY2027 revenue growth of 7.4% against our 3.0% [S0]. That is not an extravagant assumption, and it tells us the premium we measure is small rather than heroic. What makes us cautious is not the growth gap but the quality of the earnings that would have to deliver it.

The konglo lens. The engine measures the price at 1.52 times fundamental value of Rp435 and keeps part of that gap for twelve months using three regime scenarios that are independent of our business scenarios. The base regime keeps 35.0% of the premium, giving Rp638; the bear regime keeps 75.0% and gives Rp540; the bull regime gives Rp770. The probability-weighted result is our target of Rp646. This is not a fundamental call. It is a statement that a stock with a 6.4% float, HSC status and a 28.5-month free-float deadline tends to keep more of a premium than a liquid stock would, because there is no arbitrage capital able to close the gap.

One outcome is not in that table and it is the one that matters: if the controller sells down to meet the float rule inside the window, the scarcity that supports the premium disappears and the lens closes the gap completely. That full-closure path is a sensitivity, not a fourth weighted scenario: at complete closure the value is our fundamental twelve-month value of Rp486, below today's price and in SELL territory on the house bands. The target itself remains the probability-weighted three regime scenarios in the table - bear Rp540, base Rp638 and bull Rp770 - and even the bear regime keeps part of the premium rather than closing it fully. The proximity of the full-closure value to the bear regime is why we describe the rating as lens-produced: on the fundamentals alone the shares are a sell, and only the assumption that some of the premium persists for another year keeps the target above the REDUCE line.
Downside risks, with likelihood and impact:

items: **Tariff and cost squeeze (high likelihood, high impact).** Nine-month 2026 direct expenses rose faster than revenue and operating expenses rose by nearly a third, taking operating profit to IDR24.7bn on revenue of IDR169.6bn [S3]. If the tariff is not reset, every year of inflation erodes the margin further.

**Customer allocation risk (medium likelihood, high impact).** TransJakarta sets kilometres, and FY2025 shows it cutting them [S2]. A repeat of the FY2025 volume fall removes revenue against a fixed depreciation base.

**Governance and related-party risk (medium likelihood, high impact).** IDR46.7bn left the company as related-party receivables in FY2025 while IDR20.6bn of new capital came in [S4]. A structure in which minority cash funds group balances is a value leak that no DCF captures, and it is why we apply a liquidity discount.

**Free-float supply risk (high likelihood, medium impact).** A 6.4% float against a 15.0% minimum leaves a gap of 8.6% that the controller must close either by selling or by diluting [S8]. Supply arriving into a stock with IDR840.0m of daily turnover is a price event, not a liquidity event [S8].

**Liquidity risk (certain, high impact on exit).** Three-month average daily turnover of IDR840.0m and repeated zero-volume days mean an institutional position cannot be exited at the screen price [S0].

**Index and regime risk (medium likelihood, medium impact).** HSC membership removes SAFE from the IHSG and from the main index families, and MSCI has proposed Standalone status for Indonesia with a decision by 30 June 2027 [S10]. Passive demand is not coming back on the current ownership structure.
**Operational risk (medium likelihood, medium impact).** Driver turnover, accident-related unit reductions and breakdown penalties are disclosed causes of lost kilometres [S2].
**Macro and FX (medium likelihood, low-to-medium impact).** Spare parts are imported, so the rupiah at 17,633 against a house FY2027E of 18,350 raises the rupiah cost of maintenance [S11].

blocks.text: Scenarios.

The bear case cuts revenue growth and gross margin by the same amounts the bull case adds - a volume cut with a tariff squeeze, which is what the nine-month 2026 accounts already show beginning to happen [S3]. The bull case adds growth and margin on the argument that a supportive city budget and a kilometre-tariff reset do the work; the service-expansion news with TransJakarta is the evidence that volume can be added when the city pays for it [S5]. A tariff reset is a one-off level shift, so we carry it through the growth and margin shocks rather than adding a separate per-year shock that would compound every year of the forecast. Probabilities are 25% bear, 50% base and 25% bull. We do not stack a governance haircut into the bear case because we apply it as a discount in every scenario; an asymmetry in the business scenarios would double-count it.

The related-party balance is a disclosed risk that we do not model as a scenario shock, and we say why. The receivable is IDR1.5bn net at 30 September 2026 against an allowance already taken of IDR5.0bn, so even a full write-off of the remaining net balance is a rounding error against equity and moves no valuation input; the FY2025 outflow of IDR46.7bn is the tripwire to watch, not a value at risk today [S3][S4]. We attach a one-in-four probability to a further related-party outflow of that scale recurring in the forecast window, which is why it sits in the risk list rather than in the DCF.

Rating and bands. House bands put BUY at a total return of more than a quarter, ADD above a tenth, HOLD down to a loss of a tenth and REDUCE below that [S0]. Our fundamental twelve-month value of Rp486 against a price of Rp660 is a negative return of more than ten per cent, which on those bands is a REDUCE; the HOLD we publish is the lens-weighted target of Rp646 and its return of -2.1%, which sits inside the HOLD band. We state that plainly rather than dress it up: this is a float-regime hold, not an endorsement of the business at this price.

The konglo regime scenarios are separate from the business scenarios and appear in the table in the valuation section. Their spread is narrow, from Rp540 to Rp770, because the lens only decides how much of an existing premium persists, not whether the business is worth more. The risk that matters for the target is a regime change: an MSCI Standalone decision, an HSC review that escalates, or a controller selldown that breaks the float scarcity. Each compresses the premium toward fundamental value, and the base closing rate of 35.0% is the assumption a red team should attack first.

Signposts that would change our view, in order of importance: kilometre volume recovering toward the FY2024 level; a tariff reset announced by TransJakarta or the transportation agency; any renewed build in related-party receivables; and the controller's first move on the free-float requirement [S2][S4][S8].

Konglo lens versus fundamental value. The published target of Rp646 is not a fundamental value: the operating business alone is worth Rp435 a share today and Rp486 in twelve months. The gap between the target and that fundamental value is the part of the market premium the lens assumes persists in a stock with a 6.4% float and HSC status; the lens mechanics, not any governance strength, are what hold the target above the price [S8][S9].

Ownership and control. PT Infiniti Wahana holds 56.5% of 821.2 million shares, BNP Paribas Singapore Branch Wealth Management holds 27.8% through a Singapore wealth-management arrangement and PT Abdi Raharja holds 7.5% [S2]. The market data put insider ownership at 91.9% and institutional ownership at 0.0%, with free float at 6.4% [S0]. This is a controlled company in the ordinary Indonesian sense: the minority owns a claim on cash flows it cannot direct.

HSC status and index consequences. SAFE is on the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list, and from 2 November 2026 HSC stocks are excluded from the IHSG selection [S9]. The exclusion is a passive-demand event rather than a change in the operating business.

Free float. At 6.4% against a 15.0% minimum, the gap is 8.6% and the deadline is 28.5 months away [S8]. The phased schedule in the Antara article, sourced to BEI, tiers issuers by market capitalisation at 31 March 2026: larger caps face intermediate steps before the final deadline, while issuers below the threshold are given until 31 March 2029 to reach the 15.0% floor [S8]. SAFE's market capitalisation of IDR542.0bn sits in that sub-threshold small-cap tier, so the company has the single 31 March 2029 deadline and no intermediate step [S8]. The controller has sold shares once before to meet a prior float threshold in 2024, and those sales were small relative to the gap that remains [S0]. The precedent is useful: when the rule binds, the controller sells, but the time horizon gives the controller about three years to find a buyer or to inject assets.

Related parties. What we can document: IDR46.7bn of related-party receivable outflow in FY2025 [S4]; a non-preemptive capital increase approved at an extraordinary general meeting in June 2025 and settled in November 2025, issuing new shares without preemptive rights [S2][S4]; and a common-control restructuring credited to equity [S4]. A discounted private placement to affiliates is a structure flag under our own screen because it transfers value from existing minorities to the subscriber. We classify it as optics-class rather than manipulation-class because it is disclosed and shareholder-approved, but it is part of why the valuation carries a liquidity discount.

Auditor and accounts. The FY2025 statements were audited and we found no qualification in the passages we read; the group presents bus depreciation inside direct expenses, which is permitted but makes the direct-cost line opaque and is the reason the data pack's depreciation figure is wrong [S4].

Earnings-quality flags, in the form the method card requires. Accruals: net profit of IDR39.5bn against operating cash flow of IDR59.4bn implies negative accruals, which is good, but that cash flow is helped by a working-capital position that is deeply negative because payables are stretched [S4]. Cash conversion has stayed sound in 2026, with IDR42.1bn of operating cash against IDR23.6bn of net profit in nine months [S3]. IDX regime: HSC-listed, with a float below the new minimum and a history of suspension during sharp moves [S0]. Related-party gravity: IDR46.7bn of receivables in FY2025, above a fifth of revenue [S4]. Structure: one non-preemptive issuance and a share count that rose by a third to 821.2 million [S2]. Each is disclosed; none is fabrication. The composite is a name we would own only at a discount, which is what the liquidity adjustment does.

Dividend record. No cash dividend is assumed in the forecast period, and the last distributions were stock dividends in the previous century [S2]. With the controller at 56.5% a dividend would mostly be a transfer to the controlling shareholder, so its absence is not obviously adverse to minorities, but it does mean the only way to realise value is the share price.

ESG. The fleet is the exposure: diesel Volvo buses on a busway, with the company disclosing spending on pool works and preparation for electric buses [S2]. Jakarta's electrification agenda is a capex call on operators, and SAFE has no disclosed funding plan for it, which is a second reason the replacement capex in our forecast is a floor rather than a ceiling. Governance is the dominant ESG factor here, not emissions [S4].

Dated events: the FY2026 audited results test whether the margin compression of the first nine months continues, and they will show annual revenue around IDR221.7bn [S3]; the MSCI consultation feedback deadline of 30 April 2027 and the decision by 30 June 2027 on Standalone status, which hangs over the whole Indonesia small‑cap space [S10]; and the 31 March 2029 free-float deadline (the small-cap tier has this single deadline, with no intermediate step) [S8].

KPIs we watch between updates: kilometres travelled, the single best predictor of revenue; the realised bus count against the 319-unit quota; the gross margin, where the FY2026 compression is the central question; operating cash flow against net profit, which tells us whether the earnings are cash; related-party receivable balances, which we treat as a governance tripwire; and free float, which we expect to move before the deadline [S3][S4][S8].

What would make us wrong on the upside: a tariff reset that restores the FY2025 margin, a credible funded plan to fill the quota that lifts kilometres toward the FY2024 level without new equity, or a change of control that brings a mandatory tender offer above our fundamental value [S2]. What would make us wrong on the downside: another year of kilometre cuts at the customer's discretion, or a related-party balance that turns out to be unrecoverable [S4].

bear.narrative: TransJakarta trims the kilometre quota as the Jakarta subsidy is squeezed: a 3pp lower revenue growth rate in every forecast year, which compounds to a mid-teens percentage shortfall in FY2030 revenue, plus a 1.5pp gross-margin squeeze as the tariff is not indexed to fuel and wages while the fixed depreciation charge stays [S2][S3].

bull.narrative: The city raises the TransJakarta subsidy and resets the kilometre tariff: a 3pp higher revenue growth rate in every forecast year, which compounds to a low-teens revenue uplift by FY2030, plus a 1.5pp gross-margin recovery as the fixed depreciation base dilutes; the October 2026 news of resumed service supports a higher per-kilometre realisation [S5].

konglo.construction: target = fundamental 12-month value (probability-weighted business scenarios, after the liquidity discount) x the probability-weighted share of today's premium kept, (price / fundamental value today)^(1 - c) over the regime scenarios; c = share of the log gap that closes within 12 months

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: Nine months of 2026 show revenue of Rp169.6bn against Rp160.3bn a year earlier, +5.8%; we assume FY2026 revenue annualises this run-rate at 5.8% growth (Rp222bn) rather than +9% because Q4 2025 was seasonally weak and no known tariff reset supports a Q4 2026 acceleration [S3]. From FY2027 growth is allocation-only: FY2027 3% (kilometre stabilisation), then 2%, 1%, 1% (inflation indexation). The unfilled 200-unit quota contributes zero to value because no funding plan is disclosed and capex for it is not in the forecast [S2][S5].

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: Nine-month 2026 gross margin is 27.3% (gross profit Rp46.2bn on revenue Rp169.6bn) against 30.8% a year earlier, because direct expenses rose 11.3% while revenue rose 5.8% [S3]; we hold the 27.3% realised level for FY2026 and let it edge to 27.5% by FY2030 as kilometre volume stabilises against a fixed depreciation charge, but no tariff reset brings margin back toward FY2025 29.2% [S3][S4].

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Operating expenses were Rp21.5bn in nine-month 2026, 12.7% of revenue, against 10.5% a year earlier, driven by employee benefits and professional fees; we hold 12.7% for FY2026 and ease to 12% by FY2030, still above the FY2025 8.5% because the company now manages the fleet without growth [S3][S4].

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Bus depreciation FY2025 Rp30.6bn = 14.6% of revenue (Note 10 roll-forward, S4); the same fleet is depreciated straight line over 5-20 years and net book value falls about Rp7.6bn a quarter with no additions [S3], so the ratio holds while the fleet count is unchanged

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Capex was nil in FY2025 and nil in the first nine months of 2026, so FY2026 holds at nil per the last actual; fleet-replacement spend ramps from FY2027 (8% of revenue) to the 14.5% depreciation charge from FY2028 to keep the existing 119-bus fleet serviceable, funded from accumulated cash; the unfilled 200-unit quota stays unfunded because no funding plan is disclosed [S3][S4][S2].

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Hold at FY2025 actual current ratio of -40.5% (NWC = -84.9, revenue = 209.6). The 9M2026 balance sheet shows NWC of -90.89 on revenue 169.57 (-53.6%), a step change driven by lower accounts payable as debt is repaid, but we hold FY2026 at FY2025 actual -40.5% because the FY2025 level is the last full-year actual and the 9M2026 gap arises from a timing mismatch; from FY2027 we let it drift gradually toward the two-year average -45% as the cash build stops compressing payables [S4][S3].

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(tax, pbt))

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(interest_expense, debt[-1]))

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: BI rate (5.75%) less 2.75% as cash typically deposited in banks earns lower than policy rate; assume 3% nominal yield [S11]

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(minority, np))

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: No cash dividend paid historically (only stock dividends); the controller needs cash for group operations; we assume 0% payout for the forecast period [S2]

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: Long-run nominal growth of 2% for a Jakarta bus contract (no volume growth, tariff indexation below the 3.3% inflation in the macro deck), consistent with the explicit FY2030 growth path [S11]

challenges.challenge: FY2026E revenue Rp228.5bn (+9.0pct) is not the 9M run-rate the basis claims: 9M2026 revenue was +5.8pct yoy, and reaching 228.5 needs Q4 2026 +19.4pct yoy against a seasonally weak Q4 2025 (Rp49.3bn, 2pct opex, 23.7pct gross margin).
challenges.answer: Cut FY2026E revenue growth from 9.0% to 5.8% (Rp228.5bn to Rp221.7bn), annualising the delivered nine-month run-rate; the implied Q4 is at the same year-on-year rate, not +19%, and section 3 states that assumption [S3].

challenges.challenge: FY2026E capex 8pct of revenue (Rp18.3bn) is unsourced: 9M2026 and FY2025 capex are nil, and the drift justification contradicts the input basis (basis says 2pct of revenue, justification says 8pct).
challenges.answer: FY2026E capex cut from 8% to nil, matching FY2025 and 9M2026 actual; the replacement ramp starts in FY2027 at 8% and reaches 14.5% by FY2028, and basis and drift justification now agree. DCF effect of the FY2026 change alone is +Rp18.3bn of FY2026 free cash flow [S3][S4].

challenges.challenge: The EV/EBITDA cross-check capitalises FY2025A EBITDA Rp74.0bn (35.3pct margin, the peak year the report says is not repeatable) on the peer forward multiple: on our own FY2026E EBITDA of Rp66.6bn the method gives about Rp514, not Rp711, so the 25pct weight lifts the blend roughly 8pct.
challenges.answer: EV/EBITDA weight cut from 25% to 10% and DCF raised to 75%, because the method capitalises FY2025A peak EBITDA on a trailing peer multiple; section 4 labels it a peak-year cross-check against our FY2026E EBITDA. Target restated from Rp694 to Rp646 [S0][S4].

challenges.challenge: The stated COE build (rf 7.4 + 0.9x4.2 + 2.5) sums to about 13.4pct, not the 11.9pct actually used; the engine computes 7.45 - 1.62 default spread + 0.9x(4.23 + 2.46) = 11.85pct, so the key DCF input cannot be reproduced from the report.
challenges.answer: COE build rewritten exactly as the engine computes it: 7.45% risk-free less a 1.62pp sovereign default spread plus 0.9 x (4.23% mature premium + 2.46% country premium) = 11.85%, reproducing the 11.9% used [S6].

challenges.challenge: The 31 Mar 2029 free-float deadline is called the key dated risk (the controller must sell about 8.6pp of float, roughly 70m shares) but no scenario models it; the 5.1pct expected return is below the 11.9pct COE and only the lens keeping 65pct of the premium holds the target above price.
challenges.answer: Added the selldown regime: full closure of the premium gives the fundamental twelve-month value of Rp486, below price, at one-in-four probability matching the lens bear weight; section 5 tests the rating on the house bands and states that the HOLD is lens-produced, not fundamental [S8][S2].

challenges.challenge: The Rp46.7bn FY2025 related-party receivable outflow (73pct of equity) has no impairment stress in the bear case, and the section 3 claim that the 9M2026 flow was small and in the opposite direction is wrong: S3 shows a Rp1.07bn outflow, same direction.
challenges.answer: Corrected the flow direction: 9M2026 shows a Rp1.07bn outflow in the same direction, not the opposite. Disclosed the stock: Rp1.505bn net against a Rp5.003bn allowance already taken, so a 25-50% impairment is immaterial; a repeat outflow carries a one-in-four probability in the risk list [S3][S4].

challenges.challenge: Post-FY2026 growth of 5/4/4/3pct is justified by part of the 319-unit quota being filled, but the capex plan explicitly excludes the 200 unfunded buses, so the growth has no funding mechanism while the quota option also contributes zero to value.
challenges.answer: Post-FY2027 growth cut to allocation-only 3/2/1/1% with terminal growth 2%, because capex funds replacement and not the unfilled quota; section 3 states that the quota contributes zero to value and why [S2][S4].

challenges.challenge: HSC status (as of 2026-10-22), the MSCI Standalone dates (2027) and the 31 Mar 2029 deadline are cited to S2 (the 2025 annual report, which contains no MSCI or HSC mention) and S6 (an Okezone piece that states the 15pct vs 7.5pct rule but no phased 2029 schedule).
challenges.answer: Registered S8 (BEI free-float schedule via Antara: small caps 15% by 31 Mar 2029, large caps 12.5% by 2027 then 15% by 2028), S9 (HSC excluded from IHSG from 2 Nov 2026) and S10 (MSCI Standalone consultation). Frontmatter, section 6 and section 7 now cite them; SAFE HSC status comes from the konglo registry as of 2026-10-22 [S8][S9][S10].

challenges.challenge: FY2025 revenue is called a fall of -0.1pct in the investment summary and section 1 (where it is also claimed to be steeper than the -6.7pct kilometre fall, which cannot be): the actual fall is -10.3pct (S4 shows Rp233.6bn to Rp209.6bn, and the FY2025A line in the model).
challenges.answer: The -0.1% was a formatter error: revenue growth was rendered with pctv on a fraction, so -10.3% printed as -0.1%. Both occurrences now use pct and the steeper-than-kilometres claim is deleted [S4].

challenges.challenge: The bull case has no tariff-reset shock even though the per-km tariff is the biggest lever (administratively set, not reset in years) and the S5 service-expansion news is unused; the reverse DCF shows only 5.9pct FY2027 growth priced, so quota-fill upside is asymmetric and unpriced.
challenges.answer: Bull narrative and section 5 now name the kilometre-tariff reset and cite S5; the one-off level shift is carried through the mirrored growth and margin shocks because a per-year add on a rate input would compound every forecast year [S5].

challenges.challenge: The 6.7x EV/EBITDA at the current price is computed with FY2026 year-end net cash (Rp95.1bn) against today mcap; at current net cash of Rp53.4bn it is about 7.3x, so the headline multiple overstates liquidity.
challenges.answer: The 6.7x is labelled a FY2026 forward multiple on year-end net cash, and the headline also gives the trailing figure (7.0x) on current Q3 2026 net cash, so the liquidity comparison is not overstated [S0].

missing_bull_case.note: Bull case shocks only revenue growth and gross margin. The biggest lever, the administratively set per-km tariff (not reset in years, S2/S5), has no shock, and quota-fill upside is not priced (reverse DCF shows only 5.9pct FY2027 growth priced).

missing_bear_case.note: The report calls the 31 Mar 2029 float deadline the key dated risk but models it in no scenario; the Rp46.7bn related-party receivable (73pct of equity) has no impairment stress; franchise non-renewal is absent from the bear.

assumption_realism.note: FY2026E revenue +9.0pct vs the 9M run-rate +5.8pct cited in its own basis (implies Q4 +19.4pct yoy into a seasonally weak Q4 2025); post-FY2026 growth is justified by quota fill while the capex plan explicitly excludes the 200 unfunded buses.

evidence_and_citations.note: FY2025 revenue fall stated as -0.1pct in summary and section 1 (actual -10.3pct, S4); 9M2026 related-party flow called opposite direction (S3 shows same-direction Rp1.07bn outflow); HSC, MSCI and the 2029 float deadline are cited to S2 and S6 which do not contain them.

valuation_method_fit.note: COE prose (7.4 + 0.9x4.2 + 2.5) does not add up to the 11.9pct used (engine computes 7.45 - 1.62 spread + 0.9x(4.23+2.46)); EV/EBITDA cross-check on FY2025A peak EBITDA 73.95bn while the analyst forecasts 66.6bn; the 6.7x multiple mixes today mcap with FY2026 year-end cash.

bias_and_tone.note: Prose disciplined; the konglo lens is transparently separated from fundamental value and the report admits the target rests on the lens not the business. Credit - the D&A restatement and capex reset are well argued.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: Macro deck read correctly (USD/IDR 18350, cpi 3.28, gdp 5.29; terminal g 3.0pct below macro gdp); industry deck freight drivers correctly rejected for a regulated contractor.

conservatism_audit.note: Unjustified optimism - FY2026E revenue +9pct vs 9M +5.8pct. Unjustified conservatism - FY2026E capex 8pct with nil 9M2026 actual, which drifts the DCF down. Both depart from the last-actual anchor the house card requires; neither is sourced.

calibration.note: Both BLOCK flags (calibration.ebitda_margin -6.14pp, drift.capex_pct +6.5pp) carry sourced qc_justifications; QC gates run clean; no orphan justifications. The margin step-down is the realised 9M2026 trend.

signoff.notes: Round 1. The HOLD is honestly constructed and reproducible. Fundamental value today Rp435 (blend 475 = 0.75x461 + 0.10x711 + 0.15x388; x1.1185 = 531 base; scenarios 531/425/674 weighted = 540; less the 10% liquidity discount the desk should have on a 6.4% float = Rp486 twelve-month fundamental). The konglo lens then gives bear Rp540, base Rp638, bull Rp770, weighted Rp646 - I checked the arithmetic against (price/value)^(1-c) and it holds at c = 0.75/0.35/-0.10. Two things I specifically accept: (1) the report does not hide that the HOLD is lens-produced rather than fundamental, and it carries the full-closure selldown path (Rp486, below price) as a stated sensitivity; (2) the EV/EBITDA leg was cut to 10% because it capitalises the FY2025A peak margin year, which is the right call and is what my HATM comparison implies should happen more often in this batch. The two open NOTEs (Q8: Rp2.12bn bus-acquisition debt omitted from the EV bridge, 0.5% of equity value; Q9: bull narrative says low-teens where the shocks compound to mid-teens) are immaterial and should be cleaned at the next revision. No konglo group conflict: registry shows no family group for SAFE, and the regime reading matches HATM exactly (hsc-only overlay, same 0.35 base closure), which is the group consistency I required.

bias.note: FY2026E anchors on realised 9M2026: revenue +5.8% annualised, gross margin 27.3% and opex 12.7% per S3 (verified 46.22/169.57 and 21.49/169.57); capex nil per FY2025 and 9M2026 actuals; NWC held at FY2025 actual -40.5%, more conservative than the observed 9M -53.6%, on a sourced timing basis; post-FY2026 growth cut to allocation-only 3/2/1/1%. No default haircuts in either direction; both multiples capitalise peak FY2025 earnings, are disclosed as cross-checks and are down-weighted to 10%.

findings.finding: The EV-to-equity bridge uses gross cash of 53.40 as net debt -53.4 and omits the Rp2.12bn bus-acquisition debt still on the Q3-2026 balance sheet [S3]; true net cash is 51.28, so EV is about Rp2.1bn (0.5% of the Rp378.2bn equity value) too low. Immaterial to the target.

The bull narrative calls the growth shock a low-teens revenue uplift by FY2030; +3pp on FY2027-2030 on the 5.8/3/2/1/1 base path compounds to about +15.5% versus base, i.e. mid-teens. Wording only, no model effect.
